claims.text: A combined high-throughput DSC, rapid dilatometry or laser-heating, and first-principles workflow can accurately and efficiently determine fusion and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The workflow can determine melting temperature.
The workflow can determine enthalpy and entropy of fusion.
The workflow can determine volume change at melting.
The workflow can determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Single-phase high-entropy alloys can have fcc, bcc, or hcp crystal structures.
The target alloys are produced by conventional alloying methods and have homogeneous microstructures.
First-principles modeling can capture a configurational energy landscape relevant to high-entropy-alloy thermodynamics.
Measurements should use heating rates of 10–100 K/min from room temperature to above the melting point.
An oxygen-free inert or vacuum environment prevents oxidation during the measurements.
Atomic-scale configurational disorder in high-entropy alloys affects the distribution of energy states and latent heat during fusion.
The effects of configurational disorder and latent heat are quantifiable through calorimetric and dilatometric signals.
DSC records heat-flow or heat-capacity signals associated with thermal and phase behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Rapid dilatometry tracks volume change during melting of high-entropy alloys.
Coupling DSC and dilatometry with first-principles predictions permits deconvolution of latent-heat and entropy contributions and precise mapping of the melting pathway.
Measured melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change will agree with modeled predictions within ±5%.
The integrated workflow will provide reproducible and efficient screening across a range of high-entropy alloys.
Conventional fusion-property measurements examine individual alloys using slower and less efficient methods.
The proposed accuracy is primarily applicable to single-phase solid solutions, while extensive multiphase behavior or severe segregation can reduce accuracy.
Similar protocols in simpler alloy systems have demonstrated approximately ±5% accuracy.
